prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B021 as a single part with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer. The case rests on a separable pair of results. The 2011 Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model predicted flat bands at a specific twist angle, and the 2018 experiments showed correlated insulating and superconducting states at that angle, with the twist acting as a tunable control parameter. The phenomenology has since been reproduced in many laboratories and has opened a broad family of moire materials. From my own work on interfaces, the lesson that atomic registry between two layers sets the electronic state is general, and it is the kind of new capability the prize criterion of a discovery or invention points to. The citation is deliberately built on the flat-band prediction and the observed phases, not on a pairing mechanism, which answers the round-1 concern that the mechanism is unsettled. The chair's observation that most alternatives point to B021 reassures me that this is a configuration the committee can live with, although I do not treat that count as evidence about the science.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is maturity: eight years since the 2018 experiments is short beside B030 (stable for fifteen years) and B024 (a decade of replication), and the origin of superconductivity is still debated. The credit is also incomplete. Yuan Cao, first author of the 2018 papers, the independent experiments of Dean, Young, Yazdani and Efetov, and earlier moire band-structure work by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto all lie outside a three-name credit. I regard these as real costs, not footnotes. I weigh them below the clarity of the theory-plus-experiment attribution, but a member who weighs maturity first can reasonably disagree.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks (B024) have a decade of independent replication and the cleanest two-name credit, whereas B021 is young and its mechanism is unsettled.
responses.response: I accept that B024 is better confirmed and that its credit is cleaner than B021 once Cao is considered. What keeps it second for me is the question you raise yourself, namely novelty against the 2005 and 2012 prizes. A lattice clock is an extraordinary realisation of ideas honoured earlier, and its headline payoff, such as a redefinition of the second, has not yet arrived. On maturity I do not think eight years of reproduction by many independent groups makes the phases doubtful; what is young is the explanation, and the citation avoids it. I would support B024 if the committee judges that a measurement prize should come first, and I keep it as an alternative.

responses.point: B030 is the stable, mature case, and the 2016 prize concerned topological phase transitions and the integer quantum Hall effect, not time-reversal-invariant systems.
responses.response: Your distinction from 2016 is fair, and I would not oppose B030, which is why it is now my first alternative. The difficulty I cannot resolve is the one you name: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe system that Molenkamp tested, and Hasan led the 3D observations, so Kane, Mele and Molenkamp leave out people whose contributions were decisive for the experiment or for the generality of the class. A citation on quantum spin Hall alone would understate what the field became. B021 has a tighter split between prediction and observation, and its omissions, Cao and the parallel groups, are experimental follow-up and not the originating theory. If the committee can agree wording for B030 that credits the proposal and first observation only, my reservation would be smaller, but I would still rank B021 first.

responses.point: B030 is a textbook Nobel pattern, confirmed by many independent groups for nearly two decades, and the idea has proven fertile in 3D topological insulators, photonics and devices.
responses.response: I agree about the fertility and the confirmation record, and I take the chair summary's point that you and Pearce treat Mele as inseparable from Kane. That helps, but it does not remove the BHZ and Hasan problem, because the fertility you describe, 3D materials in particular, comes partly from work outside Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. The same breadth that makes B030 compelling makes any three-name credit look like a narrow slice of it. For B021 the follow-on field is wide, but the original prediction and its first demonstration are both within the credited names. I remain on B021, with B030 as the alternative I would most readily move to.

responses.point: The unresolved superconducting mechanism and sample variability mean B021 would honour a platform and phenomenology, and eight years is short for a Nobel prize.
responses.response: I agree on the substance and think our two positions are close. I would add that sample-to-sample variability is a point where my microscopy background matters: twist-angle inhomogeneity and strain are real, and they are the reason the reproducibility argument must be made about the correlated phases across groups, not about a single device. That reproducibility exists. I also share your concern about Cao. I do not see a way to credit him ahead of Jarillo-Herrero under the three-person limit, but I would want the committee record to say so explicitly. On timing, I would rather accept a young prize with a settled phenomenology than delay while an interpretation matures, since the criterion is discovery, not final understanding.

responses.point: Bistritzer should stay in the credit because the 2011 magic-angle result is the joint Bistritzer-MacDonald calculation and a third seat is available.
responses.response: I agree, and that is why I moved from two names to three after round 1. Splitting authorship of the 2011 prediction to keep the prize at two people would be hard to defend. Your own uncertainty about whether B030 can resolve its attribution problem well enough to overtake B021 is also my main test of that ballot, and so far I do not think it has.

uncertainties: Whether eight years and an unresolved superconducting mechanism make B021 premature, or whether a citation limited to the flat-band prediction and the observed phases is sufficient.
How to treat Yuan Cao and the independent groups of Dean, Young, Yazdani and Efetov, who sit outside a three-name credit.
Whether B030 could be worded and attributed so that the BHZ and Hasan omissions do not undermine it, in which case its maturity could outweigh B021.
Whether the committee prefers a new-field discovery or a measurement invention (B024) this year; I have no strong view that would justify a two-part prize.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with any shortlisted candidate or credited name. My documented connections (David R. Clarke at IBM, Chalmers colleagues, Japanese university exchanges, the microscopy federation) do not involve the credited names. The Japan links touch B024 and B005 only in a general way, and B024 is now only an alternative. Goran Johansson is also at Chalmers, which is not a conflict for B021, B030 or B024.
